context: In the decision tree, each node represents a string state. Each outgoing directed edge represents one decision: insert, delete, or replace a character. Finding the edit distance from s = hello to t = algo is equivalent to finding the shortest path from the root hello to the target algo.
description: On the left, a path runs downward through 4 string nodes connected by 3 directed edges, from s = hello at the top to t = algo at the bottom. The table lists each edge and operation in order. The first edge says only “Replace l with g.” Comparing its two strings tells us that it is the second l.

Each expanded node in the first three levels (hello, helgo, halgo) also has 3 arrows to the right pointing to ellipses “…”: without restrictions, each string admits many other edits. The omitted branches do not specify strings. The diagram illustrates the shortest-path interpretation without enumerating the entire tree.

frames.explanation: This path takes 3 edits from hello to algo, matching the edit distance of 3 given in Figure 14-27 of this section. The path alone establishes that 3 edits suffice. It cannot rule out a shorter path.
frames.title: A three-edit path from hello to algo

summary: Each node is a string, and each directed edge is one edit. Find the shortest path from hello to algo. The figure shows a three-edit path and leaves the other branches unexpanded.

tables.caption: Edits along the expanded path
rows: Replace the second l with g
